newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Socialists meet to form new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Socialists meet to form new cabinet.

text.p: The leadership of Bulgaria's ruling Socialist Party met on Sunday to try to form a new government, ignoring four weeks of daily opposition protests and calls for immediate elections.

"It will be a very dramatic meeting," said Sofia party leader Nikola Koichev. He said if the party succeeded in forming a cabinet it would be made up purely of its own members as potential coalition partners had turned down invitations to join.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) resolutely opposes any new Socialist-led cabinet and wants an immediate general election.

Several hundred opposition supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fifth day. Protesters warmed themselves at wood fires on barricades blocking the highway at Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia. There was no sign of police.

Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov said in a television interview on Saturday: "I'm sure next week Bulgaria will have a new government but it is hard to predict what the future of this government will be."

He said Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev would lead the new cabinet. Dobrev suggested on Friday that President Petar Stoyanov appoint a coalition cabinet but then put off a meeting with him, apparently under pressure from party hardliners.
Parvanov said the Socialists could count on 122 votes in parliament, an absolute majority which meant that they could win the required confidence vote.

"I think that the anti-crisis programme which is proposed by Nikolai Dobrev is quite constructive but will still need about 30 to 40 days to implement and to regain the confidence of the people," he said.

He said Bulgaria must have a government immediately to pass legislation to halt a collapse in the value of the lev, the national currency, and cope with an inflation rate which has hit 50 percent a month and is still rising.
The Socialists say they will hold general elections, not due until December 1998, later this year. Their offer failed to satisfy the opposition, which wants the vote held now.
Thousands of opposition supporters, workers and students, blaming the Socialists for the economic collapse, have staged daily anti-government rallies to demand elections.
Festive protesters, including entire families, pensioners and students, streamed through Sofia on Saturday, blowing horns, banging drums and carrying banners proclaiming: "I am not a slave."
UDF leader Ivan Kostov warned the Socialists on Saturday that similar disruptions would sweep the country if they voted in a new cabinet instead of calling elections.
"The Socialists should consider this an example of what will happen if they pass a government through parliament," he said. "The Doupnitsa road and rail blockades will become nationwide actions."
